questions.decision: Error semantics matter: transient failures and explicit access denials need different recovery paths. Preserve resilience within authority rather than treating success as the only objective.

questions.title: Reviewing the evidence, not approving the prose
questions.stem: A maintenance-risk assistant requires engineer approval before issuing a high-impact shutdown recommendation. Audits show engineers approve fluent summaries even when a cited sensor interval contradicts the recommendation. The team cannot add a second engineer to every case. It can redesign the review screen and audit a small rotating subset of cases. Which TWO changes most directly test and reduce the observed review weakness?

options.text: Require the same engineer to read the assistant's summary twice before approving, measuring only the additional time spent on review.
options.why: Reading time does not establish evidence-based judgment.

options.text: Display a larger model's agreement percentage above the recommendation, prioritizing speed for cases where the models reach the same conclusion.
options.why: Correlated model agreement can reinforce the same unsupported inference.

options.text: Show decisive sensor evidence, uncertainty and conflicting readings next to the proposed action, requiring the reviewer to resolve the contradiction.
options.why: The reviewer must assess the relevant evidence rather than prose alone.

options.text: Independently reassess a rotating subset without showing the original recommendation, comparing findings and using disagreements to improve the review process.
options.why: Blinded reassessment tests anchoring and the effectiveness of approval.

options.text: Replace source evidence with a mandatory explanation of why the engineer trusts the model, retaining the current recommendation-first screen.
options.why: A trust statement does not resolve the documented sensor contradiction.

questions.decision: Human approval is not self-validating. Make the contradictory evidence actionable and independently check whether reviewers detect errors without relying on model agreement.

questions.title: Access rights when logs contain other people
questions.stem: An EU customer submits a verified access request concerning personal data processed by an assistant. Counsel confirms the request’s scope and says the response must protect other people’s rights. Relevant data appears in source records, generated case summaries and diagnostic logs; some log entries also contain another customer’s details. Which implementation BEST satisfies the confirmed obligation without treating shared log files as indivisible disclosures?

options.text: Assemble the in-scope personal data and required processing information, applying reviewed redactions or extracts to protect other people before delivery.
options.why: The response can cover relevant derived data without exposing unrelated individuals.

options.text: Provide only the original account record, excluding generated summaries and logs because those artifacts describe system processing rather than personal data.
options.why: A derived artifact can still contain personal data within the confirmed scope.

options.text: Reject the complete access request because shared logs contain other customers, preserving confidentiality by withholding all information from the requester.
options.why: Other people’s rights do not justify automatically withholding separable in-scope data.

options.text: Export every matching raw log file because the requester’s identifier appears in it and the original request verifies their identity.
options.why: Identity verification does not authorize disclosure of another customer’s details.

questions.decision: Implement the legally confirmed access scope across actual processing artifacts while protecting others through appropriate extracts or redaction. File boundaries do not define the right.

questions.title: Useful transparency without exposing another customer
questions.stem: A consulting assistant drafts recommendations from project records. Clients cannot tell which claims are supported, and a proposed transparency page would reveal full prompts containing other clients' examples. Contract policy forbids cross-client disclosure; clients need to understand and contest recommendations rather than inspect implementation internals. The service is shared across several independently contracted clients. Which TWO changes BEST meet that need?

options.text: Clearly identify AI-assisted drafts and distinguish supported statements, assumptions and missing evidence using client-authorized source references.
options.why: This gives decision-relevant provenance within the allowed disclosure boundary.

options.text: Provide an accessible correction and escalation route, linking contested claims to an accountable consultant and a tracked resolution.
options.why: Clients can act on limitations and obtain correction.

options.text: Offer a generic AI-use disclaimer at sign-in and make internal source records available only during annual contract renewal.
options.why: A remote disclaimer and annual window do not support timely contesting of claims.

options.text: Publish the entire reusable prompt library to clients after replacing customer names, assuming this removes every confidential detail.
options.why: Name replacement does not establish that other client examples are safe.

options.text: Display the model's numeric confidence alone as a standardized explanation of why the consulting recommendation should be trusted.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence does not establish support or contestability.

questions.decision: Transparency is about meaningful provenance, limitations and recourse for the affected user. It does not require disclosing confidential prompts or another client’s records.

questions.title: Discover the acceptance boundary before the solution
questions.stem: A retail sponsor requests a product-advice chatbot to increase conversion. Store managers instead report that customers abandon orders when inventory promises differ between channels. The existing inventory system refreshes overnight, and no budget owner has agreed to change it. Marketing wants a model recommendation this week. Which discovery action BEST resolves the architectural uncertainty before promising the chatbot's business outcome?

options.text: Ask marketing to approve a conversion target for the chatbot, leaving inventory reconciliation to the implementation team after model selection.
options.why: A target without the dependency owner does not establish feasibility.

options.text: Agree the customer journey, authoritative inventory freshness and accountable acceptance metrics with marketing, stores and the inventory owner before selecting the intervention.
options.why: This tests whether the requested solution can address the observed failure.

options.text: Benchmark several models on product descriptions and use the highest conversion-intent score to select the first chatbot prototype.
options.why: Model ranking does not resolve inventory freshness or ownership.

options.text: Pilot the chatbot on existing overnight inventory data and defer discovery until enough abandoned sessions identify its production limitations.
options.why: The material freshness conflict is already known before deployment.

questions.decision: Discovery should reconcile the stated solution with the actual customer failure, authoritative dependencies and business ownership. A model benchmark cannot settle that boundary.

questions.title: An architecture decision that can be revisited
questions.stem: A call-center team compares synchronous drafting against an asynchronous enriched response. Both meet security requirements; synchronous drafting meets the current eight-second completion SLA, while enrichment improves measured resolution but completes in forty seconds. A sponsor favors enrichment for quality; operations cannot renegotiate the SLA before launch. Which TWO elements belong in the architecture decision record for this release?

options.text: Select enrichment and document its first-token latency as the evidence that the current completion-time agreement is satisfied.
options.why: First-token and completed-response latency are different obligations.

options.text: Record enrichment as a rejected launch alternative with evidence and an explicit trigger to revisit it when the service contract can change.
options.why: This preserves the trade-off and makes reconsideration evidence-driven.

options.text: Describe synchronous drafting as universally superior, omitting the enrichment evidence to avoid confusing the implementation team.
options.why: The evidence supports a context-bound decision, not universal superiority.

options.text: Defer documenting either option until after launch so the record can include a larger production sample before assigning ownership.
options.why: The implementation team needs the current decision and constraints now.

options.text: Select the feasible synchronous path for launch, recording the measured quality sacrifice and the unchanged completion SLA that controls the choice.
options.why: The release must satisfy its current hard operating constraint.

questions.decision: A useful decision record captures the selected option, rejected alternatives, evidence and conditions for change. The current SLA is decisive without erasing the other option’s value.

questions.title: A promise needs an observable endpoint
questions.stem: A claims-service contract states that the assistant should respond within five seconds, but does not define whether this means first token, completed recommendation or approval by a human. Current telemetry shows first token at one second, completion at seven and human approval at two minutes. The customer says the pilot missed its SLA; engineering says it passed. What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Revise the dashboard to show human approval latency as the single SLA metric, because it is the last stage in the process.
options.why: The final stage is not automatically the contracted obligation.

options.text: Add streaming progress messages and report the existing one-second first-token result as the pilot's contractual latency performance.
options.why: Streaming cannot resolve an undefined contractual endpoint.

options.text: Purchase more model capacity and optimize completion latency until every measured stage falls below the engineering interpretation of the target.
options.why: Optimization assumes an interpretation the customer has not accepted.

options.text: Reconcile the intended user outcome with the customer, define the latency endpoint, percentile and workload boundary, and baseline that agreed measure.
options.why: The parties are measuring different promises; clarify the contract first.

questions.decision: Expectation alignment precedes choosing the optimization target. Define what is promised and measured rather than selecting whichever existing metric supports one party.

questions.title: Handoff that preserves the reasoning
questions.stem: A platform team will hand a multilingual RAG assistant to regional support. The package includes infrastructure diagrams and deployment scripts, but regional engineers cannot determine which index revision is paired with each prompt or why a language falls back to human service. The originating team disbands next month. Which TWO additions most directly make the system maintainable after handoff?

options.text: Supply trend dashboards and a complete infrastructure inventory, asking regional teams to infer language-routing rationale from observed traffic after acceptance.
options.why: Operational metrics and inventory do not explain intended routing or reproduce the evaluated release.

options.text: Provide a searchable decision-history archive and schedule a one-day knowledge-transfer workshop, letting regional engineers reconstruct configuration relationships during incidents.
options.why: A workshop and archive help, but do not supply the missing authoritative release/configuration mapping.

options.text: Provide a versioned configuration manifest connecting prompts, models, indexes, routing thresholds and the evaluated release artifact.
options.why: Maintainers need a reproducible configuration rather than disconnected files.

options.text: Document routing rationale, escalation ownership and a tested incident/rollback exercise that the regional receiving team performs before acceptance.
options.why: This transfers operational understanding and demonstrates readiness.

options.text: Transfer all source repositories and developer contact details, treating successful access checks as evidence that regional maintainers can operate the system.
options.why: Code access is useful but does not demonstrate operational understanding or preserve the decision rationale.

questions.decision: Handoff must preserve both what is deployed and why its operational boundaries exist. Receiving-team execution demonstrates transfer better than delivery of documents alone.

questions.title: A new population is a lifecycle change
questions.stem: A document assistant was approved for English procurement contracts. Sales now proposes using it for translated employment agreements, reusing the model and retention settings to meet a customer deadline. The pipeline runs successfully on a sample, but the legal owner and evaluation team have not reviewed this use. Which lifecycle action BEST fits before committing to the new service?

options.text: Classify the change as a model upgrade and repeat only the original English procurement regression suite before deploying it.
options.why: The proposed change is in population and task, not merely model version.

options.text: Treat successful pipeline execution as sufficient continuity, adding employment examples to the next ordinary prompt-maintenance release.
options.why: Technical execution does not validate the changed use case.

options.text: Reassess the changed use and population through scoped discovery, risk review and updated acceptance ownership before committing.
options.why: The purpose and affected decisions change despite technical reuse.

options.text: Ask the customer to accept the original procurement accuracy figure and proceed under the existing internal approval record.
options.why: A customer promise cannot extend an inapplicable internal evidence boundary.

questions.decision: Lifecycle gates follow the use and risk boundary, not the amount of code changed. Reuse can reduce implementation effort without transferring acceptance evidence automatically.

questions.title: Discover disagreement in the current workflow
questions.stem: A shipping company wants to automate exception triage. Two regional teams label the same delayed shipment differently because one optimizes customer promises while the other optimizes vessel utilization. Both regional managers insist their labels are correct. The sponsor asks for a larger model trained on the combined history. What is the BEST next discovery step?

options.text: Use the larger model to relabel disputed shipments and treat its consistent answers as the new cross-region ground truth.
options.why: Consistency does not confer business policy authority.

options.text: Select the region with higher shipment volume as the source of truth, then treat the other region's labels as annotation errors.
options.why: Volume does not establish the approved objective or authority.

options.text: Resolve the regional decision objectives and escalation authority, documenting which label differences are approved operating policy rather than annotation errors.
options.why: The training target is undefined until policy disagreement is resolved.

options.text: Train on the pooled labels with region removed, using aggregate predictive accuracy to choose the most broadly acceptable policy.
options.why: Removing region hides rather than resolves competing objectives.

questions.decision: The uncertainty is normative: what counts as the right business decision. More capacity or pooled examples cannot replace stakeholder resolution of that policy.

questions.title: Feedback that does not become an uncontrolled release
questions.stem: A customer-success team sends weekly improvement requests for a production assistant. Engineers directly edit its shared prompt to keep customers satisfied; a recent edit improved one account but broke contractual response formatting for another. The service has an established incident owner but no change acceptance owner. Which TWO process changes most directly close the lifecycle gap?

options.text: Replace the shared prompt with the largest model so customer-specific edits become less likely to affect other contractual formats.
options.why: Model capacity does not define safe change governance.

options.text: Allow each account team to patch the shared prompt during its support window, collecting regressions for the next quarterly review.
options.why: This preserves uncontrolled shared changes and delayed detection.

options.text: Route accepted changes through versioned regression and affected-customer checks, with staged deployment and a defined rollback trigger.
options.why: This protects existing commitments while enabling controlled iteration.

options.text: Triage feedback against explicit use cases and contractual constraints, assigning a product/service owner authority to accept or reject proposed changes.
options.why: Requests need an accountable decision boundary rather than automatic adoption.

options.text: Require the incident owner to approve every wording change on the basis that operational accountability includes determining all product priorities.
options.why: Incident response ownership does not itself establish change acceptance authority.

questions.decision: Feedback is input to a governed change process. Separate acceptance authority from incident response and validate changes against existing commitments before expansion.

questions.title: Explain the bottleneck in the sponsor’s terms
questions.stem: A sponsor is disappointed that an assistant did not improve total delivery time. Tracing shows drafting fell from ten minutes to two, but the unchanged approval queue still averages three days. The sponsor requests another model upgrade. The pilot scope did not authorize changing that approval process. What communication BEST supports a useful next decision without overstating the pilot?

options.text: Report the 80% drafting reduction as the delivery improvement, explaining that approval latency belongs to another department's operating responsibility.
options.why: Local savings are not the same as end-to-end delivery improvement.

options.text: Recommend the largest model because higher draft quality is the most direct technical response to stakeholder dissatisfaction with delivery time.
options.why: The evidence does not show draft quality causes the queue delay.

options.text: Show measured drafting gains and the remaining approval bottleneck; compare approval-process and model investments against the agreed end-to-end delivery objective.
options.why: This connects local evidence to the unmet business outcome and alternatives.

options.text: Describe the pilot as a complete failure and return to manual drafting until a technology can eliminate the approval queue.
options.why: It discards a measured useful improvement without addressing the bottleneck.

questions.decision: Explain both the achieved component value and the unmet outcome. Architectural communication should redirect investment using the actual critical path rather than defend a local metric.

questions.title: Acceptance is demonstrated by the receiving team
questions.stem: A delivery team declares an assistant ready for operations because it passed load tests. The on-call team has the runbook but has never practiced its fallback; the external data connector has no named rotation owner. A launch date is fixed, but the contract permits a smaller staffed pilot. Which TWO actions BEST support a controlled handoff before broad release?

options.text: Assign connector credential and incident responsibilities, limiting launch scope to a staffed pilot until unresolved handoff gates are satisfied.
options.why: The reduced scope fits the contract without pretending ownership is complete.

options.text: Have the delivery team demonstrate fallback while on-call observes, retaining the existing launch scope and assigning connector ownership after the first rotation.
options.why: Observation leaves receiving-team execution untested and durable connector ownership unresolved.

options.text: Expand trace sampling and add a temporary delivery-team support channel, using incident frequency to decide when permanent ownership must be assigned.
options.why: Extra detection and temporary help do not establish the missing recovery capability or lasting responsibility.

options.text: Accept handoff against the load-test gate and schedule a receiving-team recovery exercise for the following sprint with the connector developer present.
options.why: This delays the known operational readiness gaps beyond broad exposure.

options.text: Have the receiving on-call team execute a failure-and-recovery exercise, documenting where fallback or escalation instructions fail in practice.
options.why: A runbook must work for its actual operators.

questions.decision: Handoff includes receiving-team capability and durable ownership. A permitted bounded pilot can honor timing without treating technical performance as operational acceptance.

questions.title: Guidance and enforced team boundaries
questions.stem: A company requires Claude Code to avoid production-secret directories and to use approved connectors. Its repository instructions describe those rules, but teams can change local configuration and tests show the agent can still read a protected directory. The company needs team-wide enforcement while retaining repository-specific coding guidance. Central administrators can distribute enforced settings to all enrolled teams. Which arrangement BEST fits?

options.text: Store the restrictions as a personal developer preference and ask team leads to verify that everybody copied the same configuration.
options.why: Copying personal preferences does not establish centrally enforced policy.

options.text: Add a post-run audit that detects secret reads, retaining the current access permissions so development behavior stays consistent across projects.
options.why: Detection after a read does not enforce the stated prohibition.

options.text: Enforce applicable organization-managed permission and connector controls at the team boundary; retain repository instructions for project conventions and task guidance.
options.why: Enforcement and project guidance serve different purposes.

options.text: Repeat the prohibited-directory list in every repository instruction file and rely on consistent wording to override local permission settings.
options.why: Natural-language repetition does not create an access-control boundary.

questions.decision: Instructions guide behavior; managed controls enforce applicable tool and access boundaries. Retain project guidance without treating it as a substitute for organizational policy.

questions.title: Speed the handoff between author and reviewer
questions.stem: A team uses a coding assistant to modify a payment calculation. Generated code compiles, but reviewers spend longer reconstructing assumptions than before; the initial prompt included only a terse bug title. The team wants lower total cycle time while preserving independent review and existing controls. The calculation has explicit rounding rules and boundary cases. What workflow change is the BEST next experiment?

options.text: Generate a patch and an assistant-written review checklist, asking the reviewer to approve once compilation and the checklist both report success.
options.why: Self-reported checklist success does not repair missing task context or independently establish payment behavior.

options.text: Require a detailed implementation narrative and a demonstration video while keeping the original task input and test-selection process unchanged.
options.why: Additional presentation does not directly repair the missing behavioral contract and targeted test evidence.

options.text: Provide the reproduction, expected behavior and constraints; require a bounded diff, targeted behavioral test evidence and assumptions for independent review.
options.why: It reduces reconstruction work while preserving verification responsibility.

options.text: Generate three complete implementations and ask reviewers to select the most readable one before examining the original bug reproduction.
options.why: It adds review work without repairing missing task context.

questions.decision: Optimize the complete change-and-review loop. Better task context, a bounded diff and observable evidence address the measured review bottleneck without delegating acceptance to the author.

questions.title: Debug the harness that differs from local
questions.stem: A Claude Code task passes locally but fails in CI after the first tool request. CI logs show a permission denial for its configured test runner, while the same command executes under the developer's local settings. The prompt, commit and tests are identical. Security requires keeping CI restrictions. Which TWO actions BEST isolate and repair the problem?

options.text: Provide the narrow authorized test-runner path or approved environment needed by this job, then reproduce under CI-equivalent restrictions before release.
options.why: This repairs the capability mismatch without discarding the required boundary.

options.text: Copy the developer's unrestricted personal settings into CI to make the execution environment match the successful local run exactly.
options.why: This conflicts with the retained CI restriction requirement.

options.text: Increase the reasoning budget and rerun the unchanged CI job, expecting the model to infer a command that bypasses the permission denial.
options.why: More reasoning does not grant the needed execution authority.

options.text: Remove the test step from the assistant workflow and accept compilation as equivalent evidence because the tests already pass on one workstation.
options.why: It drops the required CI validation rather than repairing its environment.

options.text: Compare the effective CI identity, tool permissions and environment configuration against local execution, preserving the denied command and request context in redacted evidence.
options.why: The observed difference is at the execution boundary, not model wording.

questions.decision: Treat tools, identities and execution policies as part of the harness under test. Reproduce the effective restricted environment and grant only the justified capability.

questions.title: A reusable skill is a maintained dependency
questions.stem: A development organization publishes a skill containing its API migration procedure. The metadata description is short, while detailed instructions load when the skill is selected. A later SDK change invalidates one migration step, and several projects follow the outdated procedure successfully enough to pass compilation. What practice BEST keeps this productivity mechanism reliable as teams reuse it?

options.text: Move the complete procedure into a shared always-loaded instruction file and ask the model to compare it against the installed SDK before editing.
options.why: Changing loading strategy does not establish an owned, validated migration procedure.

options.text: Assign ownership and version the procedure, checking representative migration behavior whenever the SDK or skill changes before promoting it for team reuse.
options.why: Reused instructions need ownership and task-level validation as dependencies evolve.

options.text: Rely on compilation as the skill's permanent acceptance gate and document the outdated step as a known limitation for future migrations.
options.why: The observed issue already survives compilation, so that gate is insufficient.

options.text: Allow project teams to fork the procedure, requiring review of each local revision but providing no central update or compatibility acceptance process.
options.why: Local review can help but leaves maintained compatibility and propagation of shared corrections unresolved.

questions.decision: Progressive loading manages context cost; it does not maintain the procedure. Versioned ownership and representative behavioral checks preserve the value of a shared skill.

drills.title: Entitlement and memory gates
drills.stem: For each situation, judge independently whether the proposed control satisfies the stated requirement. No fixed count of Yes responses is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: no licensed article use after revocation. Proposal: retain its summary but omit citations in later answers.
rows.why: Uncited use still uses the expired licensed evidence.

rows.text: Requirement: external reranking sees only authorized data. Proposal: enforce current access filters before sending candidate content to the reranker.
rows.why: Enforcement occurs before the prohibited disclosure boundary.

rows.text: Requirement: avoid durable instruction poisoning. Proposal: validate source authority and permitted effects before accepting lessons into shared memory.
rows.why: The admission gate protects the persistent instruction path.

rows.text: Requirement: legitimate optional modules remain discoverable but not executable without entitlement. Proposal: check rights only when indexing the catalog.
rows.why: Rights must be enforced at the current execution boundary.

rows.text: Requirement: accurately report translation coverage. Proposal: count all eligible requests and classify justified versus unjustified abstentions separately.
rows.why: The denominator and abstention categories expose actual coverage.

drills.title: Experiment and operating judgments
drills.stem: Decide whether each inference follows from the supplied evidence. Treat rows as independent judgments.

rows.text: A randomized offer experiment reports outcomes by assigned arm and uptake separately; this preserves the decision to offer access despite selective use.
rows.why: Assignment comparison avoids conditioning the main effect on uptake.

rows.text: The same inventory database is reused across destructive trials; model judge agreement alone removes cross-trial environment contamination.
rows.why: A judge cannot restore intended starting state.

rows.text: A report tool has lower input tokens but repeated discovery hops; end-to-end completion must be measured before claiming a speed improvement.
rows.why: Token savings do not establish full-task latency.

rows.text: A source refresh improves an index-weighted average; this establishes improvement for every supported regional user group.
rows.why: Index composition can hide degraded supported slices.

rows.text: A more accurate model creates more human escalations; complete-task cost must include review and retries before claiming overall savings.
rows.why: Per-call prices can hide downstream costs.

drills.title: Locate the primary evidence gap
drills.stem: Choose the primary missing evidence for each architectural claim. Options may repeat.

rows.text: The association claims broad value from portal answer quality but has not observed whether members have unmet questions.
rows.why: Unmet workload and user need are unestablished.

rows.text: The warehouse agent fails later trials after earlier trials consume the shared inventory database.
rows.why: Trials do not start from comparable intended state.

rows.text: A catalog finds an optional paid tool and the executor assumes discovery proves the current tenant may run it.
rows.why: Search relevance does not establish entitlement.

rows.text: The translation service reports quality only for attempted documents and hides its rise in unsupported refusals.
rows.why: The measure omits the supported-workload denominator.

rows.text: A matter server accepts a valid token and returns another matter because its shared service account can read everything.
rows.why: The token does not establish object-level delegated rights.
